title: The Bread of Life
summary: Near Passover, Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men from five barley loaves and two fish, then withdraws when they try to make him king by force, and comes to his disciples walking on the sea. The next day in the synagogue at Capernaum he tells the crowd that he himself is the bread of life come down from heaven, and that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life. Many disciples find the teaching too hard and leave, but Peter confesses that Jesus has the words of eternal life and is the Holy One of God.
story:
Chapter 5 ended in Jerusalem with the authorities seeking Jesus' life because he healed on the Sabbath and called God his own Father. Chapter 6 moves back to Galilee and to the crowds, and it traces a second kind of rejection. The authorities in Jerusalem rejected Jesus openly; here many of his own followers, who were glad to be fed, turn away when he explains what the sign means. The chapter is a sifting. It moves from a crowd of thousands, to a synagogue audience that grumbles, to disciples who leave, and finally to the Twelve, one of whom will betray him.

This is the only chapter of John set largely in Galilee after chapter 4, and it is the one place where John runs closely alongside the other Gospels. The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle besides the resurrection told in all four (Mark 6:32-44, Matthew 14:13-21, Luke 9:10-17), and in Mark and Matthew, as here, it is followed by Jesus walking on the sea. Where the others move on to Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27-30), John gives a long discourse on what the bread means and then his own version of Peter's confession (6:68-69). The chapter also brings the first of the seven sayings in which Jesus says “I am” with an image (6:35), a series that runs through the Gospel as a set of pictures of who he is, and it names the Twelve for the first time in John (6:67).
historical:
John dates the feeding by the calendar: “the Jewish Feast of the Passover was near” (6:4). This is the second of three Passovers John mentions (2:13, 6:4, 11:55), and it is the main reason the traditional count gives Jesus' public ministry two to three years. Passover, held in spring on the fourteenth and fifteenth of the month Nisan, remembered Israel's rescue from Egypt, and the whole chapter is shaped by that memory: a crowd in a wild place, bread given from God, a crossing of the sea, and grumbling like Israel's in the wilderness. John's note that there was “plenty of grass in that place” (6:10) fits the spring season, when the hills around the lake are green after the winter rains; Mark notes the green grass too (Mark 6:39).

The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long and eight wide, lying some seven hundred feet below sea level and ringed by hills, which is why sudden winds can sweep down on it (6:18). John also calls it the Sea of Tiberias (6:1, 21:1), after the city Herod Antipas founded on its western shore around AD 20 and named for the emperor Tiberius (Josephus, Antiquities 18.36-38). Josephus says Antipas built it partly on a graveyard, so that observant Jews avoided it, and the Gospels never place Jesus there, though boats from Tiberias appear in 6:23. Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome from 4 BC to AD 39, throughout Jesus' ministry. Capernaum, on the north shore, was a fishing town that the other Gospels call Jesus' own town (Matthew 9:1). The Franciscan excavators of Capernaum uncovered a white limestone synagogue that they and later archaeologists date to the late fourth or fifth century AD, built over the basalt foundations of an earlier building that Virgilio Corbo and Stanislao Loffreda identified as the synagogue of the first century; the identification is widely accepted but not certain.

The crowd's attempt to make Jesus king by force (6:15) belongs to a tense time. Rome had controlled the region since Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, and in the generation after Jesus, Josephus describes several popular leaders who drew crowds into the wilderness with promises of signs like those of Moses and Joshua. A man named Theudas led followers to the Jordan, promising to part it, in the mid-40s AD (Antiquities 20.97-98; compare Acts 5:36), and a prophet from Egypt gathered a crowd on the Mount of Olives in the 50s (Antiquities 20.169-172; Jewish War 2.261-263; compare Acts 21:38). Rome crushed both. Earlier, Judas the Galilean had led a revolt against the Roman census in AD 6 (Antiquities 18.1-10; Acts 5:37). A man who could feed thousands in the wilderness looked to some like the deliverer who would do the same, and a crowd of several thousand Galilean men on a hillside near Passover, the feast of liberation, was exactly the kind of gathering that Antipas and Rome feared. Jesus withdraws. He refuses a crown offered on those terms.

The manna was also alive in Jewish hope. A Jewish apocalypse written after the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, 2 Baruch, expects that when the Messiah is revealed the treasury of manna will come down again from on high (2 Baruch 29:8). A later rabbinic midrash, Ecclesiastes Rabbah on 1:9, sets the first redeemer, Moses, beside the last redeemer and says that as the first brought down manna, so will the last. That text is centuries later than John, but together with 2 Baruch it shows how natural the crowd's demand in 6:30-31 was: a prophet like Moses should give bread from heaven.
cultural:
Barley bread was the food of ordinary and poor people. The Mishnah, setting the minimum a husband must provide for a wife, allows twice as much barley as wheat (m. Ketubbot 5:8), which shows its lower price. The boy's five barley loaves were small flat rounds, and his two fish (opsaria, a word for fish eaten as a relish with bread) were most likely dried or pickled. Salted fish was a major industry on the lake; the town of Magdala was known in Greek as Taricheae, from the word for salting fish. Philip's reckoning of two hundred denarii (6:7) is large: a denarius was a laborer's day wage (Matthew 20:2), so the sum is some two hundred days' work, most of a year's earnings once Sabbaths and feasts are counted. Jesus puts the question to Philip, John says, to test him (6:6), and Philip was from nearby Bethsaida (1:44), the town Luke names as the setting of the feeding (Luke 9:10).

The meal follows the pattern of a Jewish meal. The head of the table took bread, spoke a blessing or thanksgiving to God, and broke and distributed it. John uses the verb eucharisteō, to give thanks (6:11, 23), the word from which the church's name for the Lord's Supper, the Eucharist, later came. The people recline (6:10), the posture of a proper meal. Gathering the leftover pieces so that nothing is wasted (6:12) reflects both Jewish respect for bread as God's gift and the story's abundance: twelve baskets of fragments from five loaves. The kophinos was a stout wicker basket that the Roman satirist Juvenal associated with Jews, who carried one with their provisions (Satires 3.14), and the number twelve recalls the tribes of Israel and the Twelve whom Jesus has chosen.

The crowd's response, calling Jesus “the Prophet who is to come into the world” (6:14), reflects the hope based on Deuteronomy 18:15-18 that God would raise up a prophet like Moses. The manna was the bread God gave Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16), and Scripture had already taught that it pointed beyond itself: God fed Israel with it to teach them that man does not live on bread alone but on every word from the mouth of the Lord (Deuteronomy 8:3). The Wisdom of Solomon, from the century before Jesus, calls the manna food of angels and bread from heaven and says it was God's word, not the harvest, that sustained his people (Wisdom 16:20-26). Philo of Alexandria, Jesus' older contemporary, went further and read the manna as the Word or Logos of God that feeds the soul (Allegorical Interpretation 3.169-176; Who Is the Heir 79). John's hearers knew this way of thinking. What they did not expect was a claim that the bread from heaven is a man whose parents they knew (6:42).

Talk of eating flesh and drinking blood would have been deeply offensive. The law forbade consuming blood, because the life is in the blood (Leviticus 17:10-14; Genesis 9:4), and eating human flesh belonged to the horrors of siege and curse (Deuteronomy 28:53-57, Lamentations 4:10). Later, pagan critics who heard garbled reports of Christian worship accused Christians of cannibal feasts, a charge that second-century defenders such as Athenagoras (Plea for the Christians 3) had to answer. The offense in 6:52 and 6:60 is real, and John does not soften it.
literary:
The chapter has three movements: a sign on the hillside (6:1-15), a second sign on the sea (6:16-21), and a long dialogue in the synagogue that moves in stages (6:22-71). The dialogue works like a sermon on a text. The crowd quotes a Scripture, “He gave them bread from heaven to eat” (6:31, drawing on Psalm 78:24 and Exodus 16:4, 15), and Jesus takes it apart phrase by phrase. It was not Moses who gave but the Father who gives; the bread from heaven is not manna but the one who comes down; and to eat it is to believe, then, more starkly, to eat his flesh. Peder Borgen (Bread from Heaven, 1965) showed that this pattern, a quoted text followed by an exposition that works through its words and closes by returning to the opening line, matches the homilies of Philo and later rabbinic sermons. A second Scripture is brought in to support the first, “And they will all be taught by God” (6:45, from Isaiah 54:13), as Jewish preachers commonly did.

Repetition carries the argument. “I am the bread of life” comes twice (6:35, 48), with variations in 6:41 and 6:51. The phrase “came down from heaven” recurs seven times, and the promise “I will raise him up at the last day” four times (6:39, 40, 44, 54), like a refrain. The verb for grumbling (gongyzō, 6:41, 43, 61) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel's murmuring against Moses over food in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7-8, Numbers 14:27), and John uses it for the crowd and then for the disciples. On the sea Jesus says, “It is I; do not be afraid” (6:20), literally ‘I am; do not fear’. The words can be an ordinary self-identification, but in a scene where he walks on the waters that in the Old Testament only God treads (Job 9:8, Psalm 77:19), John means the reader to hear more.

The chapter narrows as it goes, from five thousand, to the Jews in the synagogue (6:41, 52), to many disciples (6:60, 66), to the Twelve (6:67-71), and it ends not with Peter's confession but with a shadow: one of the Twelve is a devil. John also builds in a pattern of misunderstanding. The crowd wants bread for the stomach (6:26, 34), as the Samaritan woman wanted water for her jar (4:15), and each time Jesus draws them from the gift to the giver. Verse 6:66, “From that time on many of His disciples turned back”, marks the turning point of the Galilean ministry in John.

outline.t: Jesus feeds the five thousand and refuses to be made king
Jesus walks on the sea: “It is I”
The crowd seeks a sign; Jesus is the bread of life
The grumbling: bread that came down from heaven
Eating his flesh and drinking his blood

doctrines.note: Asked what work God requires, Jesus answers, “The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent” (6:29). Throughout the chapter coming to Jesus, believing in him, and eating the bread of life describe the same reception of him as life itself (6:35, 47), and faith is shown to be more than being impressed by signs (6:26, 36).

“Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me” (6:37), and “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him” (6:44, compare 6:65). The chapter places the Father's giving and drawing alongside the call to come and believe, and Jesus' choosing of the Twelve (6:70) includes Judas. Reformed, Arminian, Lutheran, Catholic, and Orthodox readers weigh these verses differently; see the hard question.

Jesus says it is the Father's will “that I shall lose none of those He has given Me” (6:39), and he promises that “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (6:37). Many Christians find here the security of the believer; the same chapter warns that some who followed Jesus turned back (6:66).

Four times Jesus promises to raise believers “at the last day” (6:39, 40, 44, 54). Eternal life begins now (6:47, 54) but does not replace the bodily resurrection at the end; John holds both together.

Many Christians hear the Lord's Supper in 6:51-58, though John records no institution of the meal at the Last Supper. How closely the chapter refers to the sacrament is debated; see the hard question.

words.note: Artos, bread or loaf. It occurs about 97 times in the New Testament and 24 times in John, 21 of them in this chapter. In the ancient world bread was the staple, the word could stand for food in general (as in the Lord's Prayer), and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the manna, ‘bread from heaven’. To say “I am the bread of life” (6:35) is to claim to be what a person cannot live without, not an extra.

Katabainō, to come down or descend. It occurs about 81 times in the New Testament and 17 in John, seven of them in this chapter for Jesus' coming down from heaven (6:33, 38, 41, 42, 50, 51, 58). The word marks his origin: he is not a prophet raised up from among the people but one who was with the Father and came. The crowd's objection in 6:42 is precisely that they know his family, and 6:62 answers it with the reverse movement, the Son of Man's ascent to where he was before.

Trōgō, to eat, originally to chew or munch. It occurs six times in the New Testament, four of them here (6:54, 56, 57, 58), once in John 13:18 quoting Psalm 41:9, and once in Matthew 24:38. From 6:54 John switches from the ordinary verb for eating (phagein) to this one. Some interpreters, often Catholic and Lutheran, see an emphasis on real eating that points to the Supper; others note that by the first century trōgō had become a common verb for eating and see a variation in style. Either way the language grows harder, not easier.

Sarx, flesh. It occurs about 147 times in the New Testament and 13 in John. In 1:14 “the Word became flesh”; here Jesus gives that flesh “for the life of the world” (6:51), language of sacrifice. Yet 6:63 says “the flesh profits nothing”. Most interpreters take the two uses differently: in 6:51-56 flesh is Jesus' own given body, while in 6:63 it means human nature on its own, which cannot grasp or give life apart from the Spirit.

Gongyzō, to grumble or murmur, a word that imitates the sound of low complaint. It occurs eight times in the New Testament, four in John (6:41, 43, 61; 7:32). The Greek Old Testament uses it and its noun for Israel's complaining in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7-8, Numbers 14:27). John's choice is deliberate: the crowd that asked for manna now behaves like the generation that ate it.

Helkō, to draw or drag. It occurs eight times in the New Testament: of dragging a net full of fish (21:6, 11), of drawing a sword (18:10), of dragging Paul and Silas to the authorities (Acts 16:19), and of Jesus drawing all people to himself when lifted up (12:32). In 6:44 the Father draws people to the Son. BDAG notes both a physical sense, to pull, and a figurative one, to attract. Readers who stress effectual grace point to the force of the word; others point to 12:32, where the same verb has all people as its object, and to Jeremiah 31:3, where God draws Israel with loving devotion.

Skandalizō, to cause to stumble or to offend. It occurs about 29 times in the New Testament, twice in John (6:61, 16:1). A skandalon was a trap or an obstacle that trips someone. “Does this offend you?” (6:61): Jesus' words about his flesh become the point where many disciples stumble and turn back, and in 16:1 he tells the Twelve he has warned them so that they will not stumble when persecution comes.

Zōē, life. It occurs about 135 times in the New Testament and 36 in John, more than in any other book, eleven times in this chapter. In John zōē usually means the life of God himself, shared with those who believe, often called eternal life (6:40, 47, 54). It is a present possession (6:47), sustained by the Son as bread sustains the body (6:57), and it reaches its fulfillment in resurrection (6:54). Peter's confession gathers it up: “You have the words of eternal life” (6:68).

christ:
The chapter presents Jesus as the one in whom the exodus is fulfilled and surpassed. Moses led Israel through the sea and God fed them with manna in the wilderness; Jesus feeds a multitude in a lonely place near Passover, crosses the sea in a way no one else could, and then says that he himself is the true bread God sends. The crowd rightly calls him the Prophet like Moses (6:14), but John shows he is more. Moses did not give the bread from heaven, the Father did (6:32), and the Son is not a giver of bread but the bread itself, “He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world” (6:33). Those who ate the manna died (6:49); those who eat this bread will live forever (6:58).

The walking on the sea points in the same direction. In the Old Testament God alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8) and makes his way through the waters (Psalm 77:19, in a psalm that remembers the exodus). Jesus comes to his frightened disciples across the water with the words ‘I am; do not fear’ (6:20), language that echoes God's reassurance to Israel in Isaiah 43:1-5, where God promises to be with his people when they pass through the waters. The boat's immediate arrival (6:21) recalls Psalm 107:30, where God brings storm-tossed sailors to their desired haven. This is the Lord of the sea in person.

The discourse moves from incarnation to cross. The bread “came down from heaven” (6:41), and Jesus says, “this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh” (6:51). The future tense and the word for, used in John of Jesus' death on behalf of others (10:11, 11:51-52, 15:13), look ahead to Golgotha, where his body is given. Eating his flesh and drinking his blood means receiving the crucified Christ himself as life, and the result is mutual indwelling: the one who feeds on him “remains in Me, and I in him” (6:56), the language of the vine in chapter 15. The life he gives is the life he shares with the Father (6:57).

His authority reaches past death. Four times he promises to raise believers “at the last day”, claiming as his own the work that the Old Testament reserves to God (Daniel 12:2) and that chapter 5 has already assigned to the Son (5:21, 25-29). He speaks of the Son of Man ascending to where he was before (6:62), completing the circle of descent and ascent that frames the Gospel (3:13). Finally, Peter's confession, “You are the Holy One of God” (6:69), echoes the title the demon uses in Mark 1:24 and Luke 4:34, and shows that faith is not a response to a full stomach but to Jesus himself, even when his words are hard. Judas stands in the same scene as a warning that nearness to Jesus is not the same as trust in him.
interpretation:
The church read the feeding from early on as a sign of the Eucharist. The earliest Christian art in the Roman catacombs, from the third century, shows baskets of loaves and fish, and the fifth-century mosaic floor at Tabgha on the Sea of Galilee, near the altar of the Church of the Multiplication, shows a basket of loaves between two fish. The Didache, an early church manual from around AD 100, prays over the broken bread (klasma, the word used in 6:12-13) that as it was scattered on the mountains and gathered into one, so the church may be gathered into God's kingdom (Didache 9:4). Ignatius of Antioch, writing around 110, calls the Eucharist the flesh of our Savior and the medicine of immortality (To the Smyrnaeans 7; To the Ephesians 20), language many trace to this chapter.

Augustine gave the chapter its most influential Western reading (Tractates on John 24-27, around 414). In Tractate 25 he told his hearers not to prepare their teeth and stomach but to believe, for to believe is to have eaten; in Tractate 26 he said that to believe in Christ is to eat the living bread, and he read the Father's drawing (6:44) not as force but as delight, borrowing Virgil's line that each person is drawn by his own pleasure. He also distinguished the sacrament from its reality, noting that Judas received the one without the other. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on John, read 6:51-58 plainly of the Eucharist. Thomas Aquinas, in his lectures on John, held both a spiritual eating by faith and a sacramental eating, and his office for the feast of Corpus Christi (instituted 1264), with the sequence Lauda Sion, made John 6:55-58 part of the feast's Gospel.

At the Reformation the chapter became a battlefield. In the Hussite controversy some cited 6:53 as proof that the laity must receive the cup, and the Council of Trent (Session 21, 1562) answered that John 6 has been interpreted in various ways by the fathers and does not command communion in both kinds. Luther, in The Babylonian Captivity of the Church (1520), held that John 6 does not speak of the sacrament at all but of faith in the incarnate Word. At the Marburg Colloquy (1529) Zwingli pressed 6:63, “the flesh profits nothing”, against a bodily presence in the Supper, while Luther held to the words of institution. Calvin's commentary on John (1553) says the discourse is not about the Supper but about the ongoing communion with Christ by faith that the Supper seals.

Modern critical study reopened the question. Rudolf Bultmann (Das Evangelium des Johannes, 1941) judged 6:51c-58 to be an insertion by a church editor who wanted to bring a sacramental view into a Gospel that had none; Peder Borgen (Bread from Heaven, 1965) and others answered that the whole discourse is a unified Jewish homily on Exodus 16, and Raymond Brown (The Gospel According to John I-XII, 1966) argued that the discourse speaks of revealed wisdom in its first half and of the Eucharist in its second, both the evangelist's own. The chapter holds a large place in the liturgy. The Roman Catholic lectionary interrupts the reading of Mark in Year B to read John 6 on five successive Sundays, the seventeenth through twenty-first in Ordinary Time, and the Revised Common Lectionary does the same in the summer of Year B. Suzanne Toolan's hymn I Am the Bread of Life (1966) carried the chapter's language into Catholic and Protestant worship alike.
text:
Most differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the later Greek manuscripts behind the King James Version. In verse 11 the King James Version adds that Jesus gave the bread ‘to the disciples, and the disciples to them that were set down’, words found in later manuscripts and in the parallel accounts (Matthew 14:19) but absent from the earliest. In verse 14 some early witnesses, including Papyrus 75 and Codex Vaticanus, read ‘signs’ in the plural; most read the singular. In verse 22 the King James Version adds a clause about the boat ‘whereinto his disciples were entered’, again from later manuscripts. In verse 23 the words “after the Lord had given thanks” are missing from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin and Syriac witnesses, but they are well attested and are printed in modern versions.

In verse 47 the King James Version reads ‘He that believeth on me’; the words ‘on me’ are absent from the earliest manuscripts, which have simply “he who believes”. The largest difference is in verse 69. The earliest manuscripts, including Papyri 66 and 75 and Codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, read “the Holy One of God”; later manuscripts expanded Peter's confession to match Matthew 16:16, and so the King James Version reads ‘that Christ, the Son of the living God’. Modern versions follow the earlier and harder reading. In verse 71 the best manuscripts call Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, so that Iscariot describes the father; later ones apply it to Judas, as the King James Version does, and a few, Codex Sinaiticus among them, read ‘from Kerioth’, supporting the common view that Iscariot means ‘man of Kerioth’, a town in Judah (Joshua 15:25). In verse 19, twenty-five or thirty stadia (a stadion was about 185 meters) is rendered “about three or four miles” in the BSB.

teach.big: Jesus does not merely give bread; he is the bread from heaven, given in his death for the life of the world, and he must be received by faith as life itself even when his words offend.

outline.t: Jesus meets real hunger with abundance, but he will not be made the kind of king a full stomach wants.
In the dark and the storm, the Lord of the sea comes to his disciples with his own name: I am; do not fear.
People can seek Jesus for what he gives rather than for who he is; the work God asks is to believe in the one he sent.
The true bread from heaven is a person, and the Father's will is that none given to the Son be lost and all be raised.
Grumbling at familiar origins blinds people to heavenly ones; no one comes unless the Father draws, and the bread is flesh given for the world.
Life comes only by receiving the crucified Christ himself, and it issues in mutual indwelling and resurrection.
The Spirit gives life through Jesus' words, and the same words that give life cause some to turn away.
Faith stays because there is no one else with the words of eternal life, though even among the Twelve not all believe.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first makes the feeding a lesson in sharing, as if the crowd was moved by the boy's example to bring out food it had hidden. The text gives no hint of this; it presents a sign that reveals who Jesus is, and the crowd's response (6:14-15) presumes a miracle. The second makes the chapter a promise of material provision, the very reading Jesus rejects in 6:26-27. The third turns the Eucharist question into a weapon. Teachers in every tradition should state their church's position honestly while acknowledging that faithful Christians have read 6:51-58 differently for five centuries, and should not suggest that the chapter speaks of nothing but the sacrament, or of nothing to do with it.

With 6:37-44, avoid building a full doctrine of predestination, or of its denial, from these verses alone, and avoid using them to tell anyone that they cannot come. The same passage says whoever comes will never be driven away. With 6:66 (a verse sometimes turned into numerology because of its number), keep to the point: people leave Jesus because his words are hard. And do not present the Jews of 6:41 and 6:52 as a picture of Jewish people generally; in this chapter they are a Galilean synagogue audience, and their objection is echoed by Jesus' own disciples in 6:60.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on people who are hungry in the plain sense, and it must not be spiritualized in a way that ignores them; Jesus fed the crowd before he taught it. It will also press on people who fear they have been driven away by God, or who worry that they are not among those the Father draws. The promise of 6:37 is for them: whoever comes will never be cast out, and the desire to come is itself a sign of the Father's drawing. Parents and friends of those who have walked away from faith will hear 6:66 with grief; the chapter does not hide that people leave Jesus, and it shows him asking the Twelve, not forcing them. Those who have been betrayed by someone close will notice that Jesus chose Judas and kept him among the Twelve.

hard.q: Is Jesus talking about the Lord's Supper when he speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood?
hard.a:
The case against a sacramental reading is strong. Jesus' hearers in the Capernaum synagogue could not have understood a reference to a meal not yet instituted, and John, who alone among the Gospels records no words of institution at the Last Supper, may have had reasons to keep the sacrament out of view. The chapter itself says that coming and believing bring life (6:35, 40, 47), and it ends with “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (6:63). Zwingli pressed this last verse at Marburg in 1529, and many Baptists and other evangelicals today read 6:51-58 as a vivid metaphor for believing in Jesus' death. From another direction, Rudolf Bultmann argued that the eucharistic verses were added by a later editor precisely because they do not fit the evangelist's emphasis on faith.

The case for a sacramental reading is also strong. The words flesh and blood, the shift to the more physical verb for eating, the thanksgiving over the bread (6:11, 23), the Passover setting, and the saying that his flesh is real food and his blood real drink (6:55) would have made John's first readers, who shared the Lord's Supper weekly, think of it. Ignatius of Antioch, Chrysostom, and the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches read 6:51-58 of the Eucharist, in which believers receive Christ's body and blood; Catholic scholars such as Raymond Brown have argued that the second half of the discourse is eucharistic by design. Lutherans see a connection with the real presence, though Luther himself read John 6 of faith rather than the sacrament. Calvin and the Reformed tradition hold that the chapter teaches a real feeding on Christ by faith through the Spirit, which the Supper signifies and seals, and Augustine had already said that to believe is to eat.

Most readers across these traditions agree on two points: the passage is about receiving the crucified Christ himself as life, not about a ritual performed without faith, and Christians who share the Supper can hardly hear it without thinking of the table. How directly the passage refers to the sacrament is a second-order question on which faithful churches differ.

hard.q: If no one can come unless the Father draws him, are those who do not come responsible?
hard.a:
The objection is old and serious. If coming to Jesus depends on the Father's giving and drawing (6:37, 44, 65), it seems that those who turn away (6:66) or never believe could not have done otherwise, and that God's choice rather than their own unbelief decides their fate. Skeptical readers have found here a picture of an arbitrary God, and theologians in the Arminian tradition, following Jacobus Arminius and John Wesley, have argued that a drawing that works only on some would make God the author of unbelief. They point out that in 12:32 the same verb has all people as its object: when lifted up, Jesus will draw all to himself.

The Reformed tradition, following Augustine in his later anti-Pelagian writings and Calvin, reads 6:37 and 6:44 together: all whom the Father gives will come, no one comes unless drawn, and those who come will be raised, so the drawing is effective and particular. On this view 12:32 means all kinds of people, Jew and Greek, and human responsibility is real because people refuse what they do not want (6:36, 64). D. A. Carson, in Divine Sovereignty and Human Responsibility (1981), argued that John simply holds both truths without resolving them. Arminian and Wesleyan readers teach a prevenient grace that draws all and enables each to respond, and Roman Catholic and Orthodox teaching, in differing ways, affirm that grace always goes before the human response while the response remains free. Lutheran theology affirms that conversion is God's work alone while denying that God has chosen anyone for damnation. All sides agree on what the chapter itself plainly says: salvation begins with God, no one who comes is cast out (6:37), and those who refuse are held accountable for not believing (6:36). How these fit together is a question on which faithful Christians still differ.

observe: What question does Jesus ask Philip, what do Philip and Andrew answer, and what is left over at the end?
Which Scripture does the crowd quote in 6:31, and how does Jesus correct each part of their reading of it?
What does Peter say when Jesus asks the Twelve whether they want to leave, and what does Jesus say next?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus withdrew when the crowd wanted to make him king? What kind of king were they looking for?
What is the difference between believing things about Jesus and eating his flesh, as this chapter pictures it?
How can the same chapter say that no one comes unless the Father draws him and that whoever comes will never be driven away?
apply: The crowd wanted Jesus to keep feeding them but left when he offered himself. What do you want from God more than you want God?
Peter stays not because he understands everything but because there is nowhere else to go. When has that kind of faith held you?
Where have Jesus' words offended you or seemed too hard, and what would it mean to stay with him there?
